name: X Pass
description: The X Pass is a standing guard pass that controls the upper body and knees while kicking a leg back to clear the guard, then circles to a stable top pin.
summary: The X Pass is a standing guard pass that controls the upper body and knees while kicking a leg back to clear the guard, then circles to a stable top pin.
overview:
The passer stands over a seated or supine open guard with a manageable knee line and room to retract one leg. The kick-back action clears a loose leg connection. A firmly locked half guard must be released first; chest-to-chest crossface pressure alone is a different pass.

Stay balanced over the open guard with the feet able to move. Use appropriate upper-body and knee-line grips or posts to limit the guard player following the pass. Shift weight onto the supporting leg without leaning the head beyond the base.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting — X-pass / kick-pass drill](https://www.grapplearts.com/a-guard-passing-drill-you-can-do-at-home-on-a-heavy-bag/).

attacker.overview:
The passer stands over a seated or supine open guard with a manageable knee line and room to retract one leg. The kick-back action clears a loose leg connection. A firmly locked half guard must be released first; chest-to-chest crossface pressure alone is a different pass.

Stay balanced over the open guard with the feet able to move. Use appropriate upper-body and knee-line grips or posts to limit the guard player following the pass. Shift weight onto the supporting leg without leaning the head beyond the base.

Retract the leg through available space rather than twisting a foot caught in a fixed entanglement. Move around the cleared legs while keeping the opponent's hips from tracking your path. Establish knee on belly or side control with balanced weight after the knees are fully passed.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Hip control comes from the knee-line grips and circling angle that prevent the guard player following the pass. If the finish is side control, settle balanced chest pressure only after both knees have been cleared.

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): What starting base supports the kick-pass action?
flashcards.answer: Stay balanced over the open guard with the feet able to move.
flashcards.answer_line: Stand over open guard, feet mobile

plausible: Locked half guard, chest-to-chest
Standing with ankle in tight hook
trap: Seated outside knees, feet off mat

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): What controls manage both the shoulders and knee line?
flashcards.answer: Use appropriate upper-body and knee-line grips or posts to limit the guard player following the pass.
flashcards.answer_line: Upper-body and knee grips or posts

plausible: Both hands on head, knees free
Both hands on knees, shoulders free
trap: Shoulder held, other hand on own leg

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): How do you make the passing leg light?
flashcards.answer: Shift weight onto the supporting leg without leaning the head beyond the base.
flashcards.answer_line: Shift weight onto the supporting leg

plausible: Load the leg you intend to retract
Equal foot pressure as you kick
trap: Move weight past the supporting foot

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): Which leg movement clears a loose guard connection?
flashcards.answer: Retract the leg through available space rather than twisting a foot caught in a fixed entanglement.
flashcards.answer_line: Retract leg backward into free space

plausible: Turn knee with foot still trapped
Drive foot deeper into locked legs
trap: Lift only knee, ankle stays hooked

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): After leg retraction, where do you move?
flashcards.answer: Move around the cleared legs while keeping the opponent's hips from tracking your path.

plausible: Straight back between both knees
Across one knee, far knee still in
trap: Toward chest through the knee frame

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): What must be established at the finish?
flashcards.answer: Establish knee on belly or side control with balanced weight after the knees are fully passed.

plausible: Chest pressure, both knees still in
Both ankles held, no torso contact
trap: Kick then stand clear of contact

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): What space is required before starting the kick back?
flashcards.answer: The passer stands over a seated or supine open guard with a manageable knee line and room to retract one leg.
flashcards.answer_line: Room to retract a loosely held leg

plausible: Hip room, passing ankle clamped
Upper knee free, lower foot caught
trap: Torso space, both knees clamp leg

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): Why is grinding chest pressure through locked half guard different?
flashcards.answer: The kick-back action clears a loose leg connection. A firmly locked half guard must be released first; chest-to-chest crossface pressure alone is a different pass.

plausible: Chest pressure frees ankle first
Crossed grips provide leg clearance
trap: Same finish means same pass action

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): Your ankle remains fixed as you start to kick. What next?
flashcards.answer: Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

plausible: Shift to support leg, keep kicking
Move hips around foot still hooked
trap: Drop upper grip, retract caught leg

flashcards.question: X Pass (top): Why must hip control continue after the knees are passed?
flashcards.answer: Use the circling angle and hip control to prevent the knees recovering before the upper-body pin settles.
flashcards.answer_line: They can turn and reinsert a knee

plausible: First knee clear, no far-knee path
Chest contact stops pelvic rotation
trap: Old ankle grip prevents hip turns

defender.name: X Pass Defender
defender.description: X Pass (defender): Control on the knee line plus a light passing leg signals a kick-pass attempt. Turn the hips so the knees continue facing the passer before the leg retracts.
defender.overview:
The passer stands over a seated or supine open guard with a manageable knee line and room to retract one leg. The kick-back action clears a loose leg connection. A firmly locked half guard must be released first; chest-to-chest crossface pressure alone is a different pass.

Control on the knee line plus a light passing leg signals a kick-pass attempt. Turn the hips so the knees continue facing the passer before the leg retracts. Use safe hand and foot frames to prevent upper-body collapse.

Pummel a knee or hook back inside while the passer is still outside the hip line. Frame at the shoulders and hips if the passer reaches knee on belly or side control. Release an unsafe leg hook rather than resisting a moving passer through the knee.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Make an early escape from the passing angle by keeping a forearm at the shoulder and using a short hip escape to return the knee in front of the passer. Guard retention depends on turning the knees with the hips before the upper-body pin closes.
key_principles: Read the standing grips: Control on the knee line plus a light passing leg signals a kick-pass attempt.
Keep the knees tracking: Turn the hips so the knees continue facing the passer before the leg retracts.
Maintain distance frames: Use safe hand and foot frames to prevent upper-body collapse.
Recover the leg connection: Pummel a knee or hook back inside while the passer is still outside the hip line.
Protect the landing: Frame at the shoulders and hips if the passer reaches knee on belly or side control.
Avoid twisting a trapped foot: Release an unsafe leg hook rather than resisting a moving passer through the knee.
recognition_cues: The passer stands over a seated or supine open guard with a manageable knee line and room to retract one leg.
Use appropriate upper-body and knee-line grips or posts to limit the guard player following the pass.
Retract the leg through available space rather than twisting a foot caught in a fixed entanglement.

flashcards.question: X Pass (bottom): What cue suggests the passer is preparing a kick back?
flashcards.answer: Control on the knee line plus a light passing leg signals a kick-pass attempt.

plausible: Weight sinks onto the captured leg
Knees settle with chest pressure
trap: Hands leave knees, both feet retreat

flashcards.question: X Pass (bottom): How do you keep your guard facing the passing angle?
flashcards.answer: Turn the hips so the knees continue facing the passer before the leg retracts.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn hips so knees track the passer

plausible: Leave knees behind, reach both arms
Turn shoulders, keep hips still
trap: Extend legs away, keep hip angle

flashcards.question: X Pass (bottom): What helps prevent the passer collapsing onto your upper body?
flashcards.answer: Use safe hand and foot frames to prevent upper-body collapse.

plausible: Both hands behind the passer's back
Knees away, pull their head close

flashcards.question: X Pass (bottom): When can a knee or hook restore your leg connection?
flashcards.answer: Pummel a knee or hook back inside while the passer is still outside the hip line.
flashcards.answer_line: Inside knee space before hips clear

plausible: After settled pin, no frame or space
Chest pin closed, knees still out
trap: After hip clearance without a frame

flashcards.question: X Pass (bottom): If the passer reaches your side, what should you rebuild first?
flashcards.answer: Frame at the shoulders and hips if the passer reaches knee on belly or side control.

plausible: Both arms chasing their far ankle
Pull head, flare near elbow away
trap: Old guard grip without a body frame
